keyVerseText: But the gate of the fountain repaired Shallun the son of Colhozeh, the ruler of part of Mizpah; he built it, and covered it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof, and the wall of the pool of Siloah by the king's garden, and unto the stairs that go down from the city of David.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew term כׇּל־חֹזֶה (Kol-Chôzeh) combines כֹּל (kôl), meaning 'all' or 'whole,' with חֹזֶה (chôzeh), meaning 'seer' or one who sees. Literally, this composite name suggests 'all-seeing' or 'every seer,' indicating comprehensive vision or insight. This etymology enriches the understanding of the name beyond a simple proper noun, implying a person endowed with broad perception or spiritual insight, which can be significant in a biblical context.
usageInScripture: The term כׇּל־חֹזֶה appears only twice in Scripture, both times as a proper name translated as 'of Colhozeh.' This consistent usage as a patronymic identifier, particularly linked to a figure involved in the restoration of Jerusalem’s walls, shows the word's function primarily as a personal name rather than a common noun. The limited occurrences underscore its specialized reference rather than a general concept of vision or seeing.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding כׇּל־חֹזֶה as 'all-seeing' invites reflection on God’s omniscience and the biblical theme of divine vision and insight. Although here it functions as a personal name, its root meaning echoes the spiritual truth that God sees all and guides His people with perfect knowledge. This reminds believers that those who serve in God’s work, like Colhozeh’s son Shallun in rebuilding Jerusalem, do so under the watchful providence of the all-seeing God. It also encourages faith in God’s sovereign oversight and care in the midst of restoration and renewal.
keyVerseReflection: Nehemiah 3:15 highlights Shallun, the son of Colhozeh, as a key figure in repairing the gate of the fountain and surrounding structures in Jerusalem. The mention of Colhozeh, whose name means 'all-seeing,' subtly connects the physical rebuilding with a heritage of insight and leadership. This adds depth to the verse, suggesting that the work of restoration was not random but carried out under the guidance of those who perceived God’s purposes clearly.
